query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a post-build hot isostatic pressing (HIP) cycle at 1200–1250 °C and 100–150 MPa for 2–3 h in an inert atmosphere to additively manufactured high-entropy alloy (HEA) components will reduce internal porosity, homogenize the microstructure, and relieve residual stress, resulting in higher dimensional precision and improved mechanical integrity compared to as-built parts.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured HEA components in the as-printed condition, with characteristic residual stress, microstructural inhomogeneity, and porosity.
generation.conditions: Maintaining 1200–1250 °C and 100–150 MPa for 2–3 h in an inert or argon atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Closure of internal voids and homogenization of microstructure under isostatic pressure and elevated temperature.
generation.mechanism: Under high temperature and pressure, localized plastic flow and atomic diffusion reduce or eliminate pores and cracks, smoothing out local density variations and mitigating residual stress, thereby improving the structural integrity of the HEA.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HIP-treated components will exhibit lower defect density (pore volume fraction decreased to near zero), increased dimensional accuracy, and enhanced mechanical performance (a moderate to significant increase in yield and tensile strength, depending on composition).
generation.baseline: As-printed HEA components showing notable porosity, lesser dimensional precision, and lower mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The degree of improvement may be reduced in AM builds that already have minimal porosity or for HEA compositions that are less sensitive to porosity-related defects.
generation.uncertainty: Exact magnitude of property improvement is alloy- and process-dependent; quantitative gains in strength/density are not definitively established and may vary widely among different HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Print a set of identical HEA test coupons using a consistent additive manufacturing process. Subject half of the samples to the specified HIP cycle, while leaving the other half in the as-manufactured state. Perform the same mechanical tests and microstructural examinations on both sets.
measurements: Porosity assessments (e.g., X-ray computed tomography or metallography).
Microstructure analysis (grain size, phase distribution, and defect fraction).
Mechanical tests for yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation at room and elevated temperatures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-HIP components do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in porosity or show no improvement in mechanical integrity (similar mechanical properties and dimensional stability) compared to the as-printed controls, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Efforts to enhance the microstructure and mechanical properties of additively manufactured HEAs incorporate the addition of interstitial atoms (e.g., carbon and nitrogen) to improve mechanical properties,,,, and employ nano-particle-based inoculants to refine the solidifying microstructure, thereby improving printability and mechanical behavior . Rapid solidification during L-PBF induces thermal stresses that render HEAs susceptible to hot cracking,,,,. To mitigate these issues, researchers have explored strategies such as substrate heating, and modifying scan strategies,,,. Additionally, various studies have applied post-processing techniques-such as annealing,, and hot isostatic pressing. Despite these efforts, challenges in fully eliminating hot cracking and achieving defect-free prints remain.

The Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti alloy in the form of buttons was prepared by vacuum arc melting of the nominal mixtures of the corresponding elements. The degrees of purity of Ta, Nb, Hf, Zr, and Ti were 99.9%, 99.9%, 99.7%, 99% and 99.7%, respectively. Melting was conducted in a high-purity argon atmosphere. High-purity molten titanium was used as a getter for residual oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen. In order to achieve homogeneous distribution of the elements in the alloys, the buttons were turned upside down and re-melted four times. The buttons were approximately 13 mm thick and 35 mm in diameter and had a shiny surface. Following this stage, the alloys were cast into bars of 9 mm in diameter and 85 mm in length. cited_evidence.text: Encapsulation of the mechanically alloyed powder is necessary for its compaction by HIPing. The CrFeNiTi MPEA powder (~6 g) was filled into steel tubes (V4A, 10 mm outer diameter, 0.5 mm wall thickness, 100 mm length) under an argon atmosphere, and were then sealed (Figure 4). The capsules were subjected to a pressure of 75 MPa and a temperature of 950 °C, using a hot isostatic press (EPSI, Belgium), with high purity argon gas as the pressure medium. This environment was maintained for 4 h. The cooling rate at the end of the process was moderate and reached a maximum of 12 K/min. A detailed description of the sample preparation using HIP can be found in Reiberg et al. [].

chosen.why: Hot isostatic pressing is a well-established thermal treatment that uses high pressure and temperature to densify the as-printed structure.
